lessons.title: Price First, Framework Second
lessons.summary: Separate what a chart observably shows from what the Smart Money framework calls it, so you can use SMC as a precise vocabulary without buying the folklore.
lessons.html:
Smart Money Concepts is the most popular trading framework of the last decade, and the most mythologised. Open any social feed and someone is explaining that "the banks" ran your stop, that "the algorithm" must return to a gap, that a candle you have never noticed is secretly where a fund loaded its position. Some of those people are good chart readers. Almost none of them can show you the order flow they are describing.

This course teaches SMC properly — structure, liquidity, sweeps, fair value gaps, order blocks, breakers, premium and discount, top-down timing and a complete rule-based strategy. But it teaches it with one discipline running underneath every lesson, and it is the line you will see again and again:

Price first. Framework second.

You describe what price did, in plain words that anyone could check on the chart. Only then do you apply the framework's label. If the label does not survive that order of operations, you do not use it.

What the framework actually claims

Strip away the thumbnails and SMC makes a simple argument. Large participants — banks, funds, dealers — cannot buy or sell size the way you can. A fund wanting to buy two billion euros cannot click once without moving the price against itself. So, the model says, large orders get filled where there is plenty of opposing business to trade against — and the densest opposing business sits where other traders' stop-losses and pending orders cluster: above old highs, below old lows, beyond equal highs and lows, around session extremes. Price is therefore drawn toward those clusters. When the large player is filled, price leaves quickly, and the chart is left with footprints the framework gives names to: order blocks, imbalances, breaks of structure.

That argument has three layers, and you need to know which is which.

  • Verifiable. Stop orders do cluster at obvious levels, because people are taught to put them there. Large orders are worked carefully to limit market impact. Price does frequently push beyond an obvious high or low and then reverse.
  • Plausible. Some sharp reversals after an old low is taken out may reflect a large buyer using that burst of forced selling to fill.
  • Narrative. A coordinated "smart money" entity hunting your specific stop, or a market-making algorithm that must deliver price to a level. Nobody teaching this on the internet has an audited view of institutional order flow. Neither does this course.

One chart, two descriptions

Here is the habit the whole course is built on. Look at the chart below and describe it twice.

The price-first description: price traded 24 pips below the prior low, closed back above that low on the same candle, then rose 50 pips in two candles with large bodies and small wicks, leaving a band of prices between the sweep candle's high and the third candle's low where no trading took place.

The framework description: sell-side liquidity was swept, smart money accumulated longs, displacement followed and left a bullish fair value gap.

The first description could be checked by a stranger with a ruler. The second adds a motive — accumulation by smart money — that nobody can see. Both descriptions point to the same tradeable fact: an obvious low failed to hold on a closing basis and buyers responded hard. That fact is what you trade. The motive is decoration.

KEY POINT

Write the observable description first. If the framework label adds nothing you can check on the chart, it is a story, not information.

Why a model can be useful without being literally true

None of this is a demolition job. A model does not need to describe reality literally to be useful; it needs to organise what you see and generate expectations you can test. Newtonian mechanics is "wrong" at the edges and still lands aircraft.

SMC's core observations are about price behaviour, and price behaviour you can verify candle by candle:

  • price frequently probes beyond obvious levels before reversing;
  • strong moves often retrace towards the area that launched them;
  • trends tend to announce their end by breaking structure;
  • fast one-directional moves leave gaps that are often partly revisited.

None of those needs a story about Barclays' flow desk. They are observations about where orders are likely to be and how crowds behave around obvious prices.

The danger is the causal story. A trader who believes the banks are hunting stops stops testing and starts believing. Losing trades become "manipulation" instead of data. The model becomes impossible to disprove — and a model that cannot be disproved is astrology with candlesticks.

The vocabulary, with its older names

Almost every SMC idea existed before SMC named it. That is not a criticism; it is useful, because it means decades of classical analysis apply to these concepts too.

SMC term What you can see Classical name
Liquidity pool An obvious high or low where stops are likely to sit Support / resistance with stops beyond
Liquidity sweep Price trades through a level and closes back inside False breakout, bull/bear trap, Wyckoff spring
Break of structure (BOS) A close beyond the last swing in the trend's direction Trend continuation, new higher high
Change of character (CHoCH) A close beyond the last swing against the trend Trend break, 1-2-3 reversal
Fair value gap (FVG) Candle 1's wick and candle 3's wick do not overlap Runaway gap, imbalance
Order block (OB) Last opposing candle before a strong move Demand / supply zone, "the base"
Breaker block A failed zone revisited from the other side Support turned resistance
Premium / discount Upper / lower half of the current swing Above / below the 50% retracement

SMC's genuine contribution is packaging: tighter definitions than most supply-and-demand teaching, and an explicit sequence. That sequence is the backbone of this course.

The sequence you are going to build

Every module in this course teaches one link in a chain. The chain is: bias, liquidity, sweep, shift, entry, target.

  1. Bias — the higher-timeframe trend, defined by swings (Module 1).
  2. Liquidity — where stops and pending orders are likely to cluster (Module 2).
  3. Sweep — price trades through a cluster and fails to hold beyond it (Module 2).
  4. Shift — a decisive break of structure back in the direction of the bias (Module 1).
  5. Entry — a defined zone created by the shift: a fair value gap or order block, in discount (Module 3).
  6. Target — the opposing cluster of stops (Modules 2 and 4).

Each step is a gate. If the market skips one, there is no trade. You will find that the strategy's value comes less from the setups it finds and more from the ones it refuses.

The four limits, stated up front

You are paying for honesty, so here are SMC's weaknesses before you invest twelve lessons in it.

1. Subjectivity. By its loosest definition, every wiggle has an order block. Two competent traders will mark different zones on the same chart, which makes rigorous testing hard and cherry-picked examples easy.

2. Unfalsifiability. The framework has enough optional parts that a determined believer can explain any outcome after the fact. If a zone holds, the order block worked. If it fails, price was "seeking deeper liquidity". A theory that explains everything predicts nothing.

3. Crowding. SMC is now enormously popular. Its textbook zones are drawn on hundreds of thousands of screens, which means they collect the very stop clusters the framework says get targeted. Your "smart money" entry is, statistically, a retail entry.

4. Survivorship marketing. The loudest SMC voices sell education, not audited track records. That does not prove the ideas fail. It does mean you should test them rather than trust them.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a losing trade as evidence of manipulation. Once losses become "they hunted me", nothing you do can be wrong, and nothing you do can improve. Losses are data about your rules.

How this course treats every concept

Every concept from Lesson 2 onwards gets three things:

  • An objective definition — written so that a stranger, given only your rule, would mark the same thing on the same chart. Call it the stranger test.
  • The observable reason it might matter — the order-placement or crowd-behaviour mechanism you can reason about without inside knowledge.
  • The failure case — what it looks like when the concept does not work, shown on a chart, with what you do about it.

Risk is handled the same way throughout. Every example has a stop. Position size is set from the stop distance at a fixed fraction of the account — 0.5% to 1% per trade in our illustrations — never the other way round. And every chart in this course is a training chart: illustrative, built to teach one idea clearly, not a record of a real market day.

Going deeper

Write the observation before the label. For your first month with this material, keep a two-column journal: what price did (in pips, closes, candle counts) on the left; the SMC label on the right. You will notice how often the right-hand column smuggles in certainty the left-hand column does not support — "institutional order block" where the left column only says "last down candle before a 40-pip rally". That gap is where most bad SMC trades are born.

Falsifiability as a design rule. For every rule you adopt, write down what would prove it wrong in a sample of trades. "Sweeps of the Asian low that close back inside within three M15 candles, followed by an M15 close above the last internal lower high, produce positive expectancy on EUR/USD" can be wrong, so it can be tested. "Price seeks liquidity" cannot be wrong, so it cannot be tested. Lesson 11 turns this into a backtesting protocol.

Both stories predict the same chart. For a sweep, the institutional story ("a large buyer filled into forced selling") and the mechanical story ("forced selling ran out, trapped sellers covered") predict identical candles. You do not need to know which is true to trade the pattern. You do need to know that you cannot know, so you never mistake folklore for evidence — and never size up because the story felt convincing.

Why the sequence matters more than any single concept. Each SMC element alone is weak: a gap alone is just a fast candle; an order block alone is just a candle. What gives the framework a chance of an edge is the conjunction — a sweep at an obvious level, then a structural break with real displacement, then a pullback to a defined zone in the cheap half of the range, in the direction of the higher-timeframe trend. Requiring all of them filters out most of the market. That filtering, plus the tight stop geometry it allows, is the honest case for SMC.

THE RULES
  • Describe price first in observable terms (closes, pips, candle counts); apply the SMC label second.
  • Never trade a motive you cannot see. Trade the chart event.
  • Every concept must pass the stranger test: written precisely enough that someone else would mark the same thing.
  • Every trade has a stop; size comes from the stop distance at a fixed risk of 0.5–1% of the account.
  • A loss is data about the rules, never evidence of manipulation.

Summary

  • SMC is a model of price behaviour wrapped in an institutional story you cannot verify. Learn the model; hold the story loosely.
  • Price first, framework second: write what the chart shows, then name it.
  • Most SMC concepts have older classical names; the framework's real contribution is tighter definitions and a sequence.
  • The sequence — bias, liquidity, sweep, shift, entry, target — is a chain of gates. Missing gates mean no trade.
  • The framework's weaknesses are subjectivity, unfalsifiability, crowding and marketing. Objective rules and your own testing are the cure.

lessons.title: Swing Structure and Internal Structure
lessons.summary: Mark swing points with a fixed mechanical rule, tell major swing structure from the internal ripples inside it, and identify the protected low that your bias depends on.
lessons.html:
Most SMC losses are not order-block losses or gap losses. They are structure losses. A trader sees a fifteen-minute wobble break a fifteen-minute low, calls it a "change of character", shorts a healthy four-hour uptrend and gets run over. Or the reverse: a genuine trend break gets dismissed as "just internal". Both errors have the same root. The trader never decided, in advance, which swings count.

This lesson fixes that. You will learn a mechanical rule for marking swing points, the difference between swing structure (the trend a reasonable person would describe) and internal structure (the ripples inside each leg), and the single most important level on any trending chart: the protected low (or protected high in a downtrend).

A swing point, defined so a stranger agrees

Price zigzags. Each zig ends at a swing high and each zag at a swing low. To make that objective, use one fixed rule:

  • A swing high is a candle whose high is higher than the highs of the two candles before it and the two candles after it.
  • A swing low is a candle whose low is lower than the lows of the two candles before it and the two candles after it.

This is the five-candle fractal. There is nothing magical about two candles each side — three gives fewer, larger swings — but you choose one setting and never change it mid-analysis.

Two practical points follow.

The lag is unavoidable. A swing high is not confirmed until the second candle after it closes. While price is still rising you do not have a swing high; you have a candidate. Traders who label swings at the live candle are drawing what they hope, not what the chart shows.

Not every fractal matters. On any timeframe, tiny two-pip wiggles qualify mechanically. Add a size filter: a swing only counts if the move away from it covers at least one average true range (ATR) of that timeframe. On a typical EUR/USD H1 chart that might be 10–15 pips; on H4, 25–40 pips. Use whatever your ATR shows; the point is that the filter is a number, not a feeling.

KEY POINT

A swing point needs a fixed fractal rule and a fixed size filter. Two traders using the same two settings will mark the same swings.

Swing structure: the trend you are allowed to trade

With swings marked, structure follows the classical definition. Higher highs and higher lows mean an uptrend; lower highs and lower lows mean a downtrend; anything mixed is a range.

SMC adds one important refinement. Not every swing on your chart carries equal weight. Swing structure is made of the swing points that the market has confirmed by breaking beyond the previous swing. In an uptrend:

  • A pullback low becomes a swing low only when price later closes above the previous swing high. That close is the break of structure (the subject of Lesson 3), and it proves buyers stepped in from that low.
  • Every smaller high and low that formed in between is internal structure.

That gives you a clean, objective hierarchy. The swing points are the handful of levels that define the trend. Everything else is texture.

Look at the pullback in that chart. Inside it, price made a small lower high, a lower low, another lower high and another lower low. On a lower timeframe that is a downtrend. On this timeframe, it is simply a pullback — internal structure inside one swing leg. When price eventually closed above the swing high, the pullback low was promoted to a confirmed higher low, and the uptrend continued.

Internal structure: timing, not bias

Internal structure exists in every leg by definition. Every pullback in an uptrend contains a small downtrend, and every rally in a downtrend contains a small uptrend. That means internal structure breaks every single time a pullback ends — and every time a pullback continues, internal structure confirms a "trend" that the swing chart would call noise.

If you let internal breaks change your bias, you will flip bullish and bearish several times a week on the same healthy trend. So the rule is strict:

  • Swing structure sets bias. Only a close beyond a swing point on your structural timeframe changes your view of the trend.
  • Internal structure times entries. Once you have a swing-level bias and a pullback into an area you care about, an internal break back in the direction of the bias is the signal that the pullback may be finishing. Lesson 10 builds the full top-down process around this.

The protected low and the weak high

Here is the concept that makes structure useful for trading decisions.

In an uptrend, the swing low that produced the most recent break of structure is the protected low (some teachers call it the strong low). It is protected in a literal, observable sense: it is the lowest point from which buyers drove price to a new high. While price stays above it on a closing basis, the swing uptrend is intact. A close below it is a change of character — Lesson 3.

The most recent swing high, by contrast, is the weak high. Nothing has defended it. It is simply where the last rally stopped, and stops from short-sellers plus orders from breakout buyers rest above it. In an uptrend it is the natural target. In a downtrend everything mirrors: the swing high that produced the last bearish break is the protected high; the latest swing low is the weak low.

Write both levels down every time you analyse a chart: "USD/JPY H4 — uptrend; protected low 151.14; weak high 152.56." That one line gives you a bias, an invalidation level and a destination. Every later lesson hangs off it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the most recent pullback low as protected even though it never produced a break of structure. If price has not yet closed above the prior high, that low is just internal — and a close below it says nothing about the swing trend.

Going deeper

Choosing the fractal and the size filter. Two candles each side on the structural timeframe, plus a minimum move of one ATR(14), is a sensible default. A three-candle fractal reduces false swings in choppy markets but delays confirmation by another candle. Whichever you choose, test it on at least a few hundred candles of your pair and timeframe before trading it, and write it down. Changing the swing definition to fit the chart in front of you is the most common form of hindsight bias in this framework.

Wicks for marking, closes for breaking. Mark swing points at the wick extreme, because that is where price traded. Judge breaks on candle closes on the structural timeframe. A wick beyond a swing that closes back inside is not a break of structure; Lesson 5 shows you that it is often a sweep.

Internal structure is just swing structure on a lower timeframe. The internal swings of an H4 leg are, roughly, the swing structure of the M15 chart. This is useful: it means you can do your internal analysis on M15 with the same mechanical rules, rather than squinting at tiny swings on H4. It is also dangerous: it is why traders who drop to M15 "for a closer look" start reading M15 swing breaks as if they were H4 events. Fix the role of each timeframe before the session: one sets bias, one times entries.

Ranges and the awkward middle. After a protected low breaks, the chart has no confirmed downtrend yet — it needs a lower high and a lower low of its own. In that interval the honest state is "no swing bias". SMC traders who insist on a verdict at every moment generate most of their losses in exactly this period.

Equal swings. Real charts throw up double bottoms and swings a pip or two apart. Treat lows within about a fifth of an ATR of each other as one level — and, as Lesson 4 explains, note that equal lows are precisely where stops collect.

THE RULES
  • Swing high: a high above the highs of the two candles either side. Swing low: the mirror. Confirmed only after the second candle after it closes.
  • Ignore swings whose move away is smaller than one ATR(14) of the timeframe.
  • Swing structure sets bias; internal structure only times entries.
  • In an uptrend the protected low is the swing low that produced the latest break of structure; the weak high is the latest swing high. Mirror for downtrends.
  • Mark swings at wicks; judge breaks on closes of the structural timeframe.

Summary

  • A swing point is a five-candle fractal plus an ATR size filter — objective, repeatable and confirmed with a two-candle lag.
  • Swing structure is the handful of swing points confirmed by breaks; internal structure is everything inside each leg.
  • Internal structure breaks on every pullback. It times entries; it never changes your bias.
  • The protected low (uptrend) is the trend's invalidation level; the weak high is its natural target.
  • Write bias, protected level and weak level down before you look for any trade.

quiz.q: Using the course's fractal rule, when is a swing high confirmed?
options: As soon as a red candle prints
When the second candle after it has closed with a lower high
When price returns to the previous swing low
quiz.why: The five-candle rule needs two lower highs after the candidate, so confirmation always lags by two candles.

quiz.q: Inside an H4 pullback, price breaks a small internal low. What does that tell you about the H4 swing trend?
options: Nothing yet — internal breaks happen inside every pullback
A change of character has occurred on H4
quiz.why: Internal structure breaks on every retracement by definition. Only a close beyond the protected swing low changes the swing bias.

quiz.q: Which low in an uptrend is the protected low?
options: The lowest low on the chart
Any low that touched a moving average
The swing low that produced the latest break of structure
quiz.why: The protected low is the one from which buyers drove a close above the prior swing high — the level the trend now depends on.

quiz.q: Why is the latest swing high in an uptrend called 'weak'?
options: It always breaks within five candles
It was formed on low volume
It has not been defended and stops rest above it, so it is a natural target
It is below the protected low
quiz.why: Nothing has proven it as a level; it is simply where the last rally paused, with buy-stops and breakout orders resting above.

quiz.q: A trader changes from a two-candle to a four-candle fractal halfway through analysing a chart because the new swings 'look better'. What is the problem?
options: It makes the chart too clean
It is hindsight fitting — the definition must be fixed in advance
quiz.why: Changing the rule to fit the chart in front of you is exactly the subjectivity that makes SMC untestable.

quiz.q: In the chart 'Protected low and weak high', what single line summarises the analysis?
quiz.why: Bias, invalidation level and destination — the one-line structure note every later lesson relies on.

lessons.title: BOS and CHoCH, Defined Objectively
lessons.summary: Identify a break of structure and a change of character using closes and a measurable displacement test, and tell a real shift from a wick, a marginal close or an internal wobble.
lessons.html:
"BOS" and "CHoCH" are the two most-used abbreviations in Smart Money Concepts, and the two most loosely applied. Ask five SMC traders to mark them on the same chart and you will often get five different answers, because each of them is quietly using a different definition of swing, a different idea of what "break" means, and a different timeframe.

In this lesson you will define both events so precisely that the stranger test from Lesson 1 is passed every time. You will also add the one filter that separates a market changing its mind from a market wobbling: displacement, defined with numbers rather than adjectives.

The two events in one sentence each

Using the swing points and the protected low from Lesson 2:

  • A break of structure (BOS) is a candle close beyond the most recent swing point in the direction of the trend. In an uptrend, a close above the last swing high. It confirms continuation.
  • A change of character (CHoCH) is a candle close beyond the protected swing point against the trend. In an uptrend, a close below the protected low. It revokes the trend.

Some teachers use "market structure shift" (MSS) for a CHoCH that comes with strong displacement. The label matters far less than the event. Classical traders have called the same thing a trend break, a failure swing or a 1-2-3 reversal for a century.

Break of structure: closes, not wicks

Every time a candle closes above the last swing high, two things become true at once. The uptrend has printed a break of structure, and the low that launched the move is now the protected low — the level that must hold for the trend to remain intact. Your protected low therefore moves up with each BOS, and you update it in writing each time.

Why closes rather than wicks? Because a wick beyond a swing that closes back inside shows that price was rejected beyond the level. That is not continuation; it is very often the opposite.

KEY POINT

A BOS needs a candle body to close beyond the swing on your structural timeframe. A wick beyond it that closes back inside is a rejection, not a break.

Change of character: the trend loses its licence

A CHoCH is the first close beyond the protected swing point against the trend. In an uptrend, that is a close below the protected low — the low that launched the most recent BOS.

Be precise about what this is evidence of. It is not a sell signal. It is the end of your licence to buy dips. Before the CHoCH, the market's character was "pullbacks get bought" and you were entitled to trade with it. After it, the burden of proof has moved. The trend may still resume; reversals fail often. But you no longer treat the chart as an uptrend.

Walk through that chart in order, because the order is the information:

  1. The uptrend made its last higher high, and the low at 150.94 became protected.
  2. The next rally traded above that high but closed back below it — no BOS. (Lesson 5: a sweep.)
  3. Price broke the internal low inside the range. That is an internal shift — a warning, not a verdict.
  4. Two large-bodied candles closed through the protected low. That is the swing-level CHoCH.

The sweep-first pattern — the old extreme is taken and rejected, then structure breaks the other way — is the version of a CHoCH the framework rates most highly. Its observable logic is simple: the market was tested at the extreme and failed to hold beyond it, and then failed to hold its own defended low. Two failures in a row, in a specific order.

Displacement, defined with numbers

Here is where most SMC teaching goes vague. "Displacement" gets described as "strong", "aggressive" or "impulsive" — adjectives, not rules. For this course a break qualifies as displaced when the breaking move meets all three tests:

  1. Size. The breaking candle's body (or the combined bodies of a two-candle break) is at least 1.5 times the average body size of the previous ten candles.
  2. Close quality. The breaking candle closes in the outer third of its own range — near its low for a bearish break, near its high for a bullish one.
  3. Imbalance. The move leaves at least one fair value gap (Lesson 6): the wick of the candle before it and the wick of the candle after it do not overlap.

You can argue about the exact numbers. You cannot argue about whether a given candle meets them, which is the point.

That chart shows why the filter earns its place. A close beyond the protected low by a few pips on small, overlapping candles is a rounding error with delusions of grandeur. Without the displacement test you would have flipped bearish at the low of the pullback. With it, you would have recorded "CHoCH unconfirmed — no displacement" and kept your uptrend bias, with the protected low still the reference.

COMMON MISTAKE

Calling a CHoCH on the lower timeframe and applying it to the higher one. An M15 change of character inside an H4 pullback is internal structure. It can time an entry, but it cannot overturn the H4 trend.

Practice drill

Downtrend on GBP/USD H1. Price has just closed above the high of its own small rally. Is that a reason to go long?

A worked example, in numbers

Here is how a structure note evolves through one session on an illustrative EUR/USD H1 chart. It is a teaching illustration, not a record of a real day.

  • 08:00. "Uptrend. Last swing high 1.0874. Protected low 1.0835. Weak high 1.0874." Price is pulling back.
  • 11:00. A candle closes at 1.0881, above 1.0874. Its body is 19 pips against a ten-candle average of 9; it closes 2 pips from its high; it leaves a gap between the prior candle's high and the next candle's low. BOS, displaced. New note: "Protected low moves up to 1.0852 (the pullback low that launched this break). Weak high now pending."
  • 15:00. Price pulls back to 1.0849, closing 3 pips below the protected low on a 6-pip body with no gap. Note: "Close below protected low — CHoCH unconfirmed, no displacement. Bias unchanged, under review."
  • 17:00. Price closes back above 1.0860. The unconfirmed break is now just a wick on a closing basis two candles later; the uptrend note stands.

Notice what the note does. It forces every structural claim to carry a price, a close and a displacement verdict. Nothing is "looking bearish". Either a defined event happened or it did not — and if you disagree with your own note an hour later, the note wins until a new close says otherwise.

Going deeper

Why the protected low, not just any low? Because it is the only low the market has proved matters. A protected low launched a close above the prior high, so buyers demonstrably stepped in there with enough force to extend the trend. Lows that never produced a BOS have proved nothing. Anchoring CHoCH to the protected low rather than the nearest low removes a large share of false reversals.

The awkward state after a CHoCH. A CHoCH ends the uptrend but does not create a downtrend. A downtrend needs a lower high and then a BOS below the CHoCH low. Until that happens, the honest state is "no swing bias", and the strategy in this course does not trade. The interval can be long; it is where impatient traders give back a month's work.

Measuring displacement in practice. Most charting platforms can display an average body or ATR. If yours cannot, a fast proxy is: the breaking candle is visibly the largest body of the last ten candles, closes near its extreme, and leaves a gap. Log the actual numbers in your journal for the first fifty breaks you mark. You will quickly see whether your eye agrees with the rule — and where it cheats.

Time-of-day bias in displacement. Large bodies are more common in the first hours of London and New York simply because more business is transacted then. A displaced break during the thin late-Asian hours is rarer and arguably more informative; a "displaced" break in the first five minutes after a major data release may just be the release. Lesson 10 builds session timing into the strategy.

What the framework says versus what you can see. The framework says a CHoCH marks the moment "smart money" switched sides. What you can see is that the market failed to hold the low it had most recently defended, and did so quickly. That is enough. You do not need the motive to respect the fact.

THE RULES
  • BOS = a candle close beyond the latest swing point in the trend direction. CHoCH = a candle close beyond the protected swing point against the trend.
  • Wicks do not break structure. Only closes on the structural timeframe count.
  • A CHoCH is confirmed only with displacement: body ≥ 1.5× the 10-candle average, close in the outer third of the range, and at least one fair value gap.
  • After a CHoCH the state is "no swing bias" until a new lower high and BOS (or higher low and BOS) form.
  • Lower-timeframe breaks are internal structure: they time entries and never change the higher-timeframe bias.

Summary

  • BOS: close beyond the last swing with the trend; it moves the protected level.
  • CHoCH: close beyond the protected level against the trend; it revokes the trend but does not create the opposite one.
  • Wicks beyond a swing that close back inside are rejections — often sweeps — not breaks.
  • Displacement is defined with numbers: body size, close quality, and a fair value gap.
  • The highest-quality CHoCH follows a sweep of the old extreme.

quiz.q: In an uptrend, which event is a break of structure?
options: A candle close above the last swing high
A wick above the last swing high
A close below the protected low
quiz.why: BOS requires a close beyond the latest swing point in the trend's direction. A wick alone is not a break.

quiz.q: What does a confirmed change of character in an uptrend tell you?
options: The uptrend's licence is revoked; there is no swing bias until a new structure forms
The uptrend is stronger than before
Move your stop below the next round number
quiz.why: A CHoCH ends the uptrend's character but does not by itself establish a downtrend.

quiz.q: A candle closes 3 pips below the protected low. Its body is smaller than the 10-candle average and no fair value gap forms. Under this course's rules, what is it?
quiz.why: It fails all three displacement tests, so the bias is not changed by it.

quiz.q: In the chart 'Sweep, then change of character', what happened immediately before the CHoCH?
options: A BOS above the old high
A wick above the old high that closed back below it
quiz.why: The final rally traded above the old high but closed back below — the sweep-first pattern that precedes the highest-quality CHoCH.

quiz.q: An M15 change of character occurs inside an H4 uptrend pullback, while the H4 protected low is intact. What is the H4 bias?
options: Still bullish — the M15 event is internal structure
quiz.why: Lower-timeframe breaks are internal structure. They may time an entry but cannot overturn the higher-timeframe trend.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the course's three displacement tests?
options: Close in the outer third of the candle's range
At least one fair value gap
quiz.why: Spot forex has no central volume, so the course's displacement test uses body size, close quality and imbalance only.

lessons.title: Mapping Liquidity — Where the Stops Are
lessons.summary: Mark buy-side and sell-side liquidity before the session — swing extremes, equal highs and lows, session highs and lows, trendlines and round numbers — and rank which pool is the likely draw.
lessons.html:
Every trader who has used a stop-loss has had this experience: price drops a few pips through the obvious low, takes the stop, and then rallies without you. It feels personal. It is not. Your stop was sitting where thousands of other stops were sitting, because you were all taught the same rule — "put it below the low" — and the market traded into the queue.

SMC calls those queues liquidity. This lesson teaches you to see them before price gets there, so that they become targets and warnings rather than ambushes.

What "liquidity" means on a chart

In plain market language, liquidity is the ability to trade size without moving the price much. SMC narrows the word: when an SMC trader says "liquidity", they mean a cluster of resting orders at a specific price — mostly stop-losses, plus pending breakout entries — that will turn into market orders if price touches them.

Two kinds, named for the side of the order:

  • Buy-side liquidity (BSL) rests above highs. Short sellers' stop-losses are buy orders. Breakout traders' buy-stop entries are buy orders. When price trades above an obvious high, those buy orders fire.
  • Sell-side liquidity (SSL) rests below lows. Long traders' stop-losses are sell orders, and so are breakdown sellers' sell-stop entries.

Why does it matter? Because triggered stops are fuel. A dip through a low where a few hundred long stops are queued converts them into a burst of market selling. That burst can briefly accelerate price — and it is also exactly the opposing business a large buyer needs. The framework says institutions engineer moves into these pools. What you can verify is humbler and plenty useful: price regularly travels to, and reacts around, levels where stops plausibly cluster. For trading, the humble version is enough.

KEY POINT

Liquidity is not a mysterious force. It is the queue of orders that sits beyond any level traders find obvious.

Where the queues form

Stops cluster where the textbook told everyone to put them. The list is short.

1. Swing highs and lows. Every confirmed swing high has buy-side liquidity above it; every swing low has sell-side liquidity below it. The more obvious and recent the swing, the denser the pool.

Notice that the first high's pool has already been traded through — once price moves beyond a pool, the orders have fired and the pool is gone. SMC traders call a pool that has been traded through "taken" or "swept". Only untaken pools matter for planning.

2. Equal highs and equal lows. Two or more swing points at nearly the same price. They are the most watched levels on any chart: two touches mean two generations of traders have stacked stops in the same place, and the level is drawn on a great many screens. Classical traders see "double top: resistance". SMC traders see "a pool getting deeper". Both are reading the same fact.

To keep "equal" objective, define a tolerance: on this course, two swing points count as equal if they are within 10% of the timeframe's ATR(14) of each other — roughly 2–3 pips on EUR/USD H1, 4–6 on H4.

3. Session highs and lows. The high and low of the Asian session, the London session, the previous day and the previous week are reference points for the whole professional day. Stops accumulate around them because they are the obvious "edges" that intraday traders lean on.

4. Trendlines. A rising trendline touched three times has stops under it along its whole length, because "stop below the trendline" is standard advice. That is why trendline breaks so often spike and snap back.

5. Round numbers. 1.0800, 1.2700, 150.00. Humans like round numbers, so orders cluster at and just beyond them. A round number that coincides with a swing low is a particularly crowded pool.

Ranking the pools

On any chart there are more pools than you can use. Rank them on four observable features:

  1. Obviousness. Would a beginner with a ruler see it? Equal highs, a clean double bottom and yesterday's high beat a subtle swing.
  2. Touches. Two or three touches beat one.
  3. Timeframe. An H4 swing low collects more orders than an M5 swing low.
  4. Freshness. Untaken pools only. Once traded through, a pool is spent.

The framework adds one more distinction that is genuinely useful: external versus internal liquidity. External liquidity sits beyond the current dealing range — above its swing high and below its swing low. Internal liquidity sits inside it — minor swings and fair value gaps. Price tends to alternate: from external liquidity (a sweep of a range extreme) to internal (a pullback into a gap), and from internal back to external. Lesson 9 shows how to use that rhythm to choose targets.

COMMON MISTAKE

Putting your own stop a pip beyond the most obvious level on the chart. That is the centre of the pool. Place stops beyond where a sweep would reasonably reach, and size the position down to fit the wider stop.

The pre-session liquidity map

Here is the routine, and it takes about five minutes per pair. Do it before the session, not while price is moving:

  1. On your structural timeframe (H4), mark the untaken swing high and swing low of the current range — external liquidity.
  2. Mark any equal highs or lows within the last 100 candles.
  3. Mark the previous day's high and low, and the previous week's high and low if they are within reach.
  4. On the entry timeframe (M15), mark the Asian session high and low once Asia closes.
  5. Note any round number within those levels.
  6. For each level write one line: who has stops here, and which way would they push price?

A level identified calmly in advance is analysis. A level "discovered" while price is racing towards it is usually adrenaline doing the drawing.

A worked map, in numbers

An illustration of the routine on GBP/USD before the London open — invented numbers, chosen for clarity:

  • H4 external liquidity. Range high 1.2788 (buy-side above), range low 1.2642 (sell-side below). H4 trend: up, protected low 1.2642.
  • Equal highs. Two H1 highs at 1.2760 and 1.2762 — within 10% of the 24-pip H1 ATR, so they count as equal. Buy-side pool above 1.2762.
  • Previous day. High 1.2771, low 1.2698.
  • Asia. High 1.2733, low 1.2711 — a 22-pip range.
  • Round numbers. 1.2700 sits 2 pips beneath yesterday's low: a crowded sell-side pool.

Now the one-line notes. "Above 1.2733: Asian-range shorts' stops and breakout buys. Above 1.2762: deeper pool, equal highs. Above 1.2788: H4 external buy-side — the draw if the uptrend continues. Below 1.2711: Asian-range longs' stops. Below 1.2698/1.2700: yesterday's low plus round number — the most crowded sell-side pool on the chart."

With an H4 uptrend, the plan almost writes itself: the counter-trend pools at 1.2711 and 1.2698 are where a pullback might sweep; the with-trend pools at 1.2762 and 1.2788 are the targets. You have not predicted anything. You have simply listed where the orders are likely to be — and therefore where the market's reactions are most likely to happen.

Going deeper

Draw on liquidity. Given a higher-timeframe bias, the framework asks: which untaken external pool is price most likely travelling towards? In an uptrend, it is usually the buy-side liquidity above the weak high (Lesson 2). That pool is your target, and also the reason you do not short just beneath it — price has an obvious reason to get there. The counter-trend pool, the sell-side below a recent low, is the one a pullback might sweep before continuing. Lesson 5 is about exactly that event.

Why obviousness is the mechanism. Every item on the list is a level that is obvious. That is not a coincidence. Obviousness is what concentrates orders, and concentrated orders are what create both the fuel and the reaction. A level nobody can see collects no stops and therefore holds no fuel. If you need three indicators and a custom drawing to find a "liquidity level", it is not one.

The crowding twist. As SMC has become popular, its own favourite levels — the edge of a famous order block, the far side of a fair value gap — are now obvious too, and are collecting stops of their own. Keep that in mind when a textbook-perfect zone fails by a few pips and then reverses. That is the same mechanism, applied to the framework's own followers.

Stop placement arithmetic. Suppose the obvious low is 1.0850 and sweeps on your pair typically reach 5–10 pips beyond such a level. A stop at 1.0848 is in the pool; a stop at 1.0838 is beyond most sweeps. If your account risk is 1% and the wider stop is 22 pips instead of 12, the position simply becomes smaller: risk stays fixed in money, size flexes. Never tighten the stop to keep the size.

THE RULES
  • Mark liquidity before the session on the structural and entry timeframes.
  • Buy-side liquidity sits above highs; sell-side liquidity sits below lows. Only untaken pools count.
  • Equal highs/lows: swing points within 10% of ATR(14) of each other.
  • Rank pools by obviousness, touches, timeframe and freshness.
  • Never place your own stop inside an obvious pool; size the position to the wider stop.

Summary

  • Liquidity in SMC means clusters of resting stop and breakout orders at obvious prices.
  • Buy-side liquidity sits above highs; sell-side below lows. Pools vanish once price trades through them.
  • The main pools: swing extremes, equal highs and lows, session extremes, trendlines and round numbers.
  • Rank pools by obviousness, touches, timeframe and freshness; separate external from internal liquidity.
  • The untaken pool in the direction of your bias is the natural target; the counter-trend pool is where a pullback may sweep.

quiz.q: What does 'buy-side liquidity' refer to?
options: Banks' buy orders below the market
Orders placed during the Asian session
Resting buy orders — short sellers' stops and breakout buys — above highs
quiz.why: Stops on short positions and buy-stop entries are buy orders, and they rest above obvious highs.

quiz.q: Two swing highs on EUR/USD H1 are 2 pips apart and ATR(14) is 24 pips. Under the course rule, are they equal highs?
options: Only if a third high forms
quiz.why: 10% of 24 pips is 2.4 pips; a 2-pip difference is within tolerance.

quiz.q: In the session chart, what happened to the Asian low at the London open?
options: Price traded through it, then reversed and later took the Asian high
quiz.why: London traded through the obvious Asian low — where stops sat — then reversed and ran to the opposite pool.

quiz.q: Which pool is the most likely target for an uptrend, all else equal?
options: The sell-side liquidity under the protected low
The middle of the Asian range
The untaken buy-side liquidity above the weak high
quiz.why: With an uptrend bias, the untaken buy-side pool above the weak high is the natural draw.

quiz.q: Why is 'stop one pip below the obvious low' poor placement?
options: It sits in the centre of the sell-side pool that sweeps commonly reach
Stops should always be at round numbers
quiz.why: The obvious low is exactly where stops cluster. Place stops beyond typical sweep reach and size down.

quiz.q: Which statement keeps 'price first, framework second'?
options: Liquidity is a hidden force only professionals can see
Price frequently trades to obvious levels where stops plausibly cluster
The algorithm must take every pool
quiz.why: That is the observable, testable version. The others assert intent or obligation nobody can verify.

lessons.title: Liquidity Sweeps — Failed Breaks You Can Measure
lessons.summary: Recognise a liquidity sweep with objective rules, tell it apart from a genuine breakout using the close, displacement and context tests, and place stops beyond the sweep rather than inside the pool.
lessons.html:
You now have a liquidity map: the pools of stops above highs and below lows. This lesson is about what happens when price reaches one.

Sometimes price trades through the pool and keeps going. That is a breakout, and trends are made of them. Sometimes price trades through the pool, fires the orders, and snaps straight back. That is a liquidity sweep — in classical language a false breakout, a bull or bear trap, or in Wyckoff's terms a spring or upthrust. Telling the two apart, with rules rather than hope, is one of the most valuable skills in this course.

Anatomy of a sweep

A sweep has four observable parts. Learn them in order.

  1. A pool. An obvious level from your map — here, equal lows with sell-side liquidity beneath them.
  2. A trade through. Price trades beyond the level by at least a pip or two. The stops fire.
  3. A close back inside. The candle (or one of the next two candles) closes back on the original side of the level.
  4. Displacement away. Price then moves away from the level with the size, close quality and imbalance you defined in Lesson 3.

The framework tells this story as "smart money ran the sell stops to fill buy orders". The mechanical story is: forced selling below the lows ran out; with no genuine follow-through selling, price fell back inside; traders who had sold the break were now trapped and their exits added fuel to the rally. Both stories predict exactly the same candles. You cannot know which is true, and you do not need to. You trade the four observable parts.

The objective definition

For this course, a sweep is:

  • price trades beyond a marked pool by at least 1 pip, and
  • a candle on the timeframe where the pool was marked closes back inside the level within three candles of the first trade-through, and
  • the furthest point beyond the level is less than one ATR(14) of that timeframe. Beyond that distance the market has simply broken out and then retraced, which is a different event.

That last clause matters. Without a depth limit, any breakout that eventually comes back can be rebranded a sweep after the fact.

KEY POINT

A sweep is a failed break: through the pool, back inside within three candles, and less than one ATR deep. If any part is missing, it is not a sweep.

Sweep or breakout? Three tests

Here is the uncomfortable truth that most SMC content skips: most pushes through a level are not sweeps. Trends are a series of old highs being taken and held. If you fade every poke through a high you are trading against trends, and the market will invoice you for it.

So the working question is never "was that a stop hunt?" It is "did the break hold?" Three observable tests answer it.

1. The close. A sweep fails to close beyond the level, or closes beyond and is engulfed within three candles. A genuine breakout closes decisively beyond and stays there.

2. Displacement. After a genuine sweep, the move back away from the level is fast, large-bodied and one-directional — it meets the Lesson 3 displacement test. A hesitant drift back inside on small overlapping candles is not confirmation. It is noise, and often the pause before the breakout resumes.

3. Context. A sweep of a low inside an established uptrend, during a pullback into the cheaper half of the range, is a far better candidate than a sweep against a freight-train trend on the back of a major news release. Counter-trend sweeps exist, but they need more evidence, not less.

That chart is a losing trade, and it was a poor trade before it lost. The candle passed the sweep definition; the context failed. That is why a sweep, on its own, is never an entry in this course. It is one gate in the sequence — bias, liquidity, sweep, shift, entry, target.

The stop-hunt myth, and why it matters to you

The phrase "stop hunt" implies intent: someone hunted you. In the retail imagination that becomes "my broker hunts my stops", which, for a regulated broker in a market as deep as EUR/USD, is somewhere between implausible and absurd for retail-sized positions. What actually happened is simpler and more useful: you placed your stop where everyone places stops, and the queue got filled.

This is not just fairness to brokers. A trader who believes they were hunted feels wronged, and wronged traders revenge-trade. A trader who sees that they parked their stop in a crowded pool feels mildly embarrassed, and embarrassed traders adjust. The adjustment is practical:

Place stops beyond the sweep wick plus a buffer (this course uses about 10% of the structural timeframe's ATR), not a tidy pip under the swing low. Then size the position for that wider stop. Risk stays fixed at 0.5–1% of the account; the lot size flexes.

COMMON MISTAKE

Entering on the sweep candle itself. The candle that closes back inside tells you the break failed; it does not tell you the reversal has started. Wait for the shift — Lesson 3's displaced CHoCH on the entry timeframe — before you commit.

Practice drill

GBP/USD M15, ranging. Price has just traded above a set of equal highs and closed back below them. Short now?

A worked example, in numbers

An illustration with invented numbers. EUR/USD, H4 uptrend, protected low 1.0790. On the M15 chart, the Asian session low is 1.0846 and the previous day's low is 1.0843 — a crowded sell-side pool just above the round number 1.0840. M15 ATR is 8 pips.

At 08:15 London time price trades to 1.0838, five pips through the Asian low and three through yesterday's low, triggering the stops beneath both. The 08:15 candle closes at 1.0849, back above both levels. Depth beyond the pool: 5 pips, less than one M15 ATR. Close back inside: the same candle. Sweep confirmed by definition.

That is all it is so far. The plan now waits for the next gate — an M15 close above the pullback's last internal lower high at 1.0861, with displacement. If it comes, the stop for any long goes below the sweep wick plus a buffer: 1.0838 minus about 10% of H4 ATR (here, 3 pips), so 1.0835. If instead the next candles close back below 1.0843 and stay there, the event becomes a breakdown, the sweep label is withdrawn, and you do nothing.

Two outcomes, both pre-written before the candle closed. That is the difference between reading a sweep and hoping for one.

Going deeper

Session timing as a soft filter. Sweeps of the Asian range around the London open, and of the London morning extreme around the New York open, are staples of SMC teaching. The kernel of truth is mundane: those transitions concentrate order flow, so obvious levels get tested when participation surges. Treat timing as mild confluence, not a law — and test it on your pairs before you rely on it. Lesson 10 defines the windows this course uses.

Multi-candle sweeps. On the timeframe where the pool is marked, a sweep is often one wick. On a lower timeframe the same event is a short run beyond the level, a stall and a sharp reversal — complete with its own internal structure. That is why the definition allows up to three candles to close back inside, and why you always judge the sweep on the timeframe where the pool lives.

Depth. Track how far beyond the level your sweeps travel on your pair and timeframe. On a typical H1 major, most will reach a fraction of an ATR. If your data shows sweeps commonly reaching half an ATR, your stop buffer must be outside that distance, or you will be swept along with the pool.

Classical evidence. Because a sweep is a false breakout, everything published on false breakouts is evidence about sweeps — including the well-known "turtle soup" pattern in classical trading literature, which fades failed breaks of 20-day extremes. A concept with two names and one body of evidence is stronger than a concept with one name and a social media following.

Location is the real prize. Entering after a sweep and shift puts you near the extreme of the move, with a logical invalidation just beyond the swept wick. When it works, the distance to the opposing pool is large relative to that stop. That geometry — not secret knowledge — is the honest reason serious traders bother with the pattern.

THE RULES
  • Sweep = trade-through of a marked pool by at least 1 pip, close back inside within three candles, depth less than one ATR(14).
  • A close beyond that holds for three candles is a breakout, not a sweep.
  • A sweep is a gate, never an entry. Wait for a displaced shift on the entry timeframe.
  • Counter-trend sweeps against a clean higher-timeframe trend are not traded in this strategy.
  • Stops go beyond the sweep wick plus a buffer of about 10% of ATR; size the position to the stop.

Summary

  • A sweep has four observable parts: pool, trade-through, close back inside, displacement.
  • The objective definition adds a three-candle limit and a one-ATR depth limit, so breakouts cannot be rebranded after the fact.
  • Most breaks are not sweeps. Close, displacement and context decide.
  • The stop-hunt story is unnecessary and psychologically harmful; the practical lesson is to keep your stop out of the pool.
  • A sweep is one gate in the sequence. On its own it is not a trade.

quiz.q: Which sequence describes a sweep in the order it happens?
options: Pool, trade-through, close back inside, displacement
Close back inside, pool, displacement, trade-through
quiz.why: Pool, trade-through, close back inside, displacement — all four observable on the chart.

quiz.q: Price closes 18 pips above a range high, holds above it for the next six candles and retests it successfully. What is it?
options: A breakout — no close back inside within three candles
quiz.why: Without a close back inside within three candles, the definition of a sweep is not met. It held, so it is a breakout.

quiz.q: Why does the course cap sweep depth at one ATR?
options: Because sweeps are always exactly one ATR
To stop breakouts that later retrace from being relabelled as sweeps
quiz.why: Without a depth limit, any failed breakout could be called a sweep after the fact — the unfalsifiability problem.

quiz.q: In the counter-trend example on USD/JPY, why was the long a poor trade before it lost?
options: The H1 trend was a clean downtrend and the bounce had no displacement
quiz.why: Context failed: a sweep against a clean trend, without displacement, is not a setup in this strategy.

quiz.q: Where should your stop go on a long after a sell-side sweep?
options: One pip below the original swing low
Beyond the sweep wick plus a buffer of about 10% of ATR
At the nearest round number above entry
quiz.why: The original low is the centre of the pool. Beyond the sweep wick plus a buffer is the logical invalidation.

quiz.q: In the drill, what was missing before a short could be considered?
options: A displaced shift lower and a bearish higher-timeframe bias
quiz.why: A sweep is a gate, not an entry. Without a shift and bias there is no trade — and the level then broke out.

lessons.title: Fair Value Gaps — The Most Objective Tool in SMC
lessons.summary: Mark bullish and bearish fair value gaps with the three-candle rule, choose an entry convention in advance, and know when a gap has failed.
lessons.html:
Most SMC concepts involve some judgement. Which swing counts? Which candle is the order block? Where does the dealing range start? The fair value gap is the exception. It is defined by three candles and one comparison, and two traders looking at the same chart will mark exactly the same gaps every time.

That makes it the best tool in the framework for building rules you can test. It also makes it the easiest to abuse, because gaps are everywhere and they look like slots waiting for a coin. This lesson gives you the definition, the three honest uses, and the failure case.

The three-candle definition

Take any three consecutive candles.

  • A bullish fair value gap exists when the high of candle 1 is below the low of candle 3. The prices between them were traded only by candle 2, in one direction, on the way up.
  • A bearish fair value gap exists when the low of candle 1 is above the high of candle 3.

The gap is the zone between candle 1's wick and candle 3's wick. No artistic licence, no redrawing.

To keep the tool useful, add two objective filters:

  1. Size. Ignore gaps smaller than 10% of the timeframe's ATR(14). On M1 and M5 charts, tiny gaps form by the dozen every hour and most are microstructure noise.
  2. Status. A gap is fresh until price trades back into it. It is filled when price trades through to the far edge (candle 1's wick). It is invalid when a candle closes beyond the far edge.
KEY POINT

Bullish FVG: candle 1 high below candle 3 low. Bearish FVG: candle 1 low above candle 3 high. The gap is the zone between those two wicks — nothing else.

What the framework says, and what you can see

The framework's story: price moved so one-sidedly that only one side of the market was transacting — an "imbalance" — so the market will later be "drawn back" to rebalance those "inefficiently priced" levels.

Hold that loosely. Markets are not obliged to repair anything, and no exchange mechanism requires a gap to be revisited. What you can verify is simpler: fast moves are frequently retraced in part, because fast moves overshoot, early buyers take profit, and the market breathes. When a retracement enters the gap, it revisits the footprint of the original urgency. If that urgency came from persistent interest, the revisit often finds it again. Same behaviour, no metaphysics.

Three honest uses, in order of importance

1. As evidence that displacement was real. This is the most valuable use and the least discussed. Overlapping candles mean two-way trade; two-way trade means no urgency. A move that leaves one or more gaps is telling you participation was genuinely one-sided. That is why the Lesson 3 displacement test requires a gap. In practice: the gap is the evidence, and the order block (Lesson 7) is the inference.

2. As an entry zone after a shift. After a displaced change of character, the playbook waits for price to retrace into the gap that the displacement left and enters there, with the stop beyond the swept extreme that started the move.

3. As a target — modestly. An obvious unfilled gap is on many screens, and price frequently trades back into gaps. But be honest about the base rate. In a strong trend, gaps can sit unfilled for weeks while price runs away. "It has to fill the imbalance" has funded many a stubborn counter-trend position. A gap is a tendency, not a debt the market owes you.

Choosing an entry convention — once

Price does not owe the gap a full fill. Strong moves often retrace a quarter or a third of a gap and leave. That creates a genuine, unresolvable trade-off:

  • Near edge (candle 3's wick): filled most often, worst price, widest stop in R terms.
  • Midpoint (the framework calls it "consequent encroachment"; we will just say midpoint): a balance.
  • Far edge (candle 1's wick): best price, fewest fills — and you will miss the strongest moves by construction.

There is no correct answer here, only a consistent one. This course's default is the midpoint, because it balances fill rate against stop size, but your own backtest (Lesson 11) should decide. What you must never do is choose the convention trade by trade, after you can see how price behaved. That is hindsight wearing a lab coat.

When a gap fails

A bullish gap is invalid once a candle closes below candle 1's high — the far edge. At that point the urgency it recorded has been fully reversed, and any long based on it is wrong.

Notice two things about that loss. First, it was a 1R loss, as planned — the stop was set before entry and sized at a fixed fraction of the account. Second, there was nothing in the gap itself that warned of failure. The gap in that chart had no sweep before it and no higher-timeframe bias behind it. Context ranks the gap; the gap does not rank itself. That is the most important sentence in this lesson.

COMMON MISTAKE

Trading every gap. A gap in the middle of nowhere, with no sweep before it and no structural break, is just a place where price once moved quickly. If you cannot say in one sentence why this gap exists, skip it.

A worked example: grading three gaps

Suppose an illustrative GBP/USD M15 chart, H4 trend up, shows three bullish gaps this morning:

  • Gap A — 4 pips, formed at 03:00 during a quiet Asian drift. M15 ATR is 9 pips, so the size filter (10% of ATR, about 1 pip) is passed, but there was no sweep before it and no structure broke. Grade: context-free. Skip.
  • Gap B — 11 pips, formed at 08:20 by the two large candles that followed a sweep of the Asian low and closed above the pullback's last internal lower high. Grade: sweep, displaced shift, with-trend. This is the entry candidate.
  • Gap C — 6 pips, formed at 09:10 near the top of the same rally, already 40 pips above the sweep low. Grade: valid but late; it sits in the expensive half of the new leg (Lesson 9). Watch, do not trade.

Gap B's midpoint becomes the limit entry. The stop goes below the sweep wick plus a buffer, not below the gap, because the gap is only the entry location — the sweep low is the invalidation. Target: the untaken buy-side pool above the H4 weak high.

Three gaps, one trade. That ratio is normal, and it is the point: the tool is objective, but your selection must be just as objective.

Going deeper

Timeframe discipline. A four-hour gap and a one-minute gap are different objects with different lifespans. Hopping between timeframes until you find a gap that justifies the trade you already want is the framework's most popular form of self-deception. Fix your timeframes in advance: in this course, H4 gaps are context and targets; M15 gaps created by the shift are entries; M1 is optional refinement only.

Stacked gaps. Very strong displacement often leaves two or three gaps in a row. The highest-quality entry is usually the gap nearest the origin of the move (the deepest one), because it sits closest to your invalidation and in the cheapest part of the leg — Lesson 9 makes this precise with premium and discount. The shallowest gap gets filled more often but buys less reward per unit of risk.

Inverse gaps. When a gap fails — a candle closes through its far edge — some traders flip it: a failed bullish gap becomes potential resistance on a retest from below. This is the same logic as the breaker block (Lesson 8) and the classical "support becomes resistance". It is testable; treat it as an optional variant, not a core rule.

Gaps on the weekend open. True price gaps between Friday's close and Monday's open are a different thing — a jump in quoted price with no trading at all. Do not confuse them with fair value gaps, which form during continuous trading. Mixing the two in a backtest will distort your results.

What to log. For each gap you trade or watch: size in pips and as a fraction of ATR, whether a sweep preceded it, whether it broke structure, how deep the retrace went (as a percentage of the gap), and the outcome in R. After fifty examples you will know more about gaps on your pair than any thumbnail can tell you.

THE RULES
  • Bullish FVG: candle 1 high below candle 3 low. Bearish FVG: candle 1 low above candle 3 high.
  • Ignore gaps smaller than 10% of ATR(14) on the timeframe.
  • A gap is invalid when a candle closes beyond its far edge.
  • Only trade gaps created by a displaced shift that followed a sweep, in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  • Choose one entry convention (default: midpoint) before testing and never change it trade by trade.

Summary

  • The fair value gap is the most objective SMC tool: three candles, one comparison.
  • Its best use is as evidence of real displacement; its workhorse use is as an entry after a shift; its weakest use is as a target.
  • Gaps are often only partly filled. Choose near edge, midpoint or far edge in advance and accept the trade-off.
  • A close beyond the far edge invalidates the gap.
  • Context — sweep, shift, bias — ranks the gap. The gap does not rank itself.

quiz.q: Which condition defines a bullish fair value gap?
options: Candle 2 is the largest green candle
Candle 1's low is above candle 3's high
Three green candles in a row
Candle 1's high is below candle 3's low
quiz.why: The bullish gap is the space between candle 1's high and candle 3's low that only candle 2 traded through.

quiz.q: When is a bullish gap invalid under the course rules?
options: When it is more than ten candles old
When a candle closes below candle 1's high (the far edge)
quiz.why: A close beyond the far edge means the urgency the gap recorded has been fully reversed.

quiz.q: In the shallow-fill example, why did a far-edge limit order miss the trade?
options: Price only retraced into the top quarter of the gap before continuing
quiz.why: Strong trends often fill only part of a gap. Far-edge entries buy better prices at the cost of missing these moves.

quiz.q: What is the most valuable use of a fair value gap according to this lesson?
options: As evidence that a move had genuine displacement
As a stand-alone entry anywhere on the chart
quiz.why: Gaps prove one-sided participation. That is why displacement requires one and why gaps confirm order blocks.

quiz.q: A gap forms in the middle of a range with no sweep before it and no structural break. What should you do?
options: Skip it — context ranks the gap
Enter at the far edge with a tight stop
quiz.why: A gap without a sweep, shift or bias is just a place price once moved quickly.

quiz.q: Which statement keeps 'price first, framework second'?
options: The algorithm must rebalance every gap
Gaps show exactly where banks bought
Fast moves are often partly retraced, and gaps record where the move was one-sided
Unfilled gaps are debts the market must repay
quiz.why: That is the observable description. Obligation and identity claims are narrative.

lessons.title: Order Blocks — An Objective Definition and a Grading System
lessons.summary: Mark order blocks with a rule a stranger could follow, grade them A, B or C on displacement, sweep and structure, and trade only fresh A-grade blocks with a pre-planned failure case.
lessons.html:
The order block is the most famous idea in Smart Money Concepts and the most abused. In its loosest form — "the last opposite candle before a move" — it describes almost every candle on every chart. Mark them all and you get the wallpaper you saw in Lesson 1, where every bounce "respects a block" and nothing is ever wrong.

This lesson does three things. It gives you a definition precise enough to pass the stranger test. It adds a grading system so you mark a handful of blocks instead of dozens. And it shows you, in advance, what a failed block looks like and what you do about it.

What an order block is — and what it is called elsewhere

A bullish order block is the last down-closing candle (or tight run of down-closing candles) before a displaced move upwards. A bearish order block is the last up-closing candle (or run) before a displaced move downwards. You draw a zone across that candle's range and watch what happens when price returns.

The model says this candle marks where large participants filled: the last flush of selling was them buying into it, and when price returns, their remaining interest — or their defence of the position — produces a reaction.

What you can verify is a chart-level regularity: strong moves frequently retrace towards their origin, and the origin frequently produces a reaction. If that sounds familiar, it should. It is a demand zone — "the base before the breakout" — with a sharper definition. The sharper definition is genuinely helpful. The causal story is genuinely unprovable. Take the definition; leave the theology.

The objective definition

For a bullish order block, all of the following must be true (mirror everything for bearish):

  1. The candle. The last candle that closed lower than it opened before the up-move. If two or three consecutive down candles form the base, the block is the whole run.
  2. The displacement. The move away meets the Lesson 3 displacement test — large bodies, strong closes — and leaves at least one fair value gap. No gap, no block.
  3. The zone. From the block's highest high to its lowest low. (A common variant uses open-to-low; pick one and keep it.)
  4. Fresh. Price has not traded back into the zone since it formed.
  5. Invalidation. A candle close below the zone's low ends the block.

Look at the order of events in that chart. The block is not special because a candle is red. It is special because of what came after it: a displaced move that left a gap and broke structure. Without those, the red candle is just a red candle.

KEY POINT

The fair value gap is the evidence; the order block is the inference. No gap above a bullish block means no block.

Grading: A, B or C

By the raw definition, blocks are still common. Grading is what stops the concept collapsing into confirmation bias. Score each candidate on three criteria, in writing, before price returns:

  • Sweep. Did the block (or the move into it) take out an obvious pool — a prior low, equal lows, the Asian low? A block born from a sweep has a clean story even in classical language: the failed break trapped sellers, their exits fuelled the rally, and the origin is a level the market has already proved it will defend.
  • Structure. Did the displacement break structure — a BOS with the trend, or a displaced CHoCH? A block that launched a structural break outranks one that produced a wobble inside a range.
  • Gap. Required for any grade at all, as above. Larger gaps, or stacked gaps, are better evidence.

Then:

  • A-grade: gap + sweep + structural break, fresh. Tradeable.
  • B-grade: gap + one of sweep or structure, fresh. Watch; trade only if your own testing supports it.
  • C-grade: anything else. Do not mark it at all.

You will mark far fewer zones. That is the point. A trader with three A-grade blocks on the chart has a plan. A trader with fifteen unrated blocks has a horoscope.

Refinement and the first touch

Refinement. An H4 block might span 60 pips — hopeless for precise risk. The usual fix is to drop to a lower timeframe and find the meaningful structure inside the parent zone: the sweep wick, a tight base, or an unfilled gap within the block. Some traders also use the block's 50% level (the "mean threshold") as a line in the sand: reactions from the upper half of a bullish block are acceptable; a clean close through the midpoint is a warning. All defensible, all testable, none sacred. Pick one convention and keep it.

Mitigation simply means price has returned to the block. The first touch is the trade the model cares about. By the second or third visit the zone has been used — on either story you prefer — and it has become an obvious level in its own right, which (Lesson 4) means it is now collecting stops. This course trades first touches only.

Trading an A-grade block

Here is a bearish example, so you see the mirror image.

The plan, written before the touch:

  • Entry: limit at the near half of the block (here 151.86), after the zone has been graded A.
  • Stop: beyond the block's far edge plus a buffer of about 10% of ATR — here 152.02, six pips above the 151.96 high.
  • Target: the next untaken opposing pool — here the sell-side liquidity beneath the displacement leg's low, 151.20. Reward 66 pips against 16 pips of risk: about 4R if completed, which is generous because the stop was unusually tight. Most A-grade trades offer 2–3R.
  • Size: 0.5–1% of the account divided by the 16-pip stop.
  • Failure plan: a close above 151.96 ends the block. The stop is already beyond it.

The failure case — planned, not discovered

Here is a block that failed, and why it should not have been traded.

At the zone your job is binary and pre-written: reaction with displacement, or decisive close through. Decide your response to each before the touch. Deciding during it is how "the zone will hold" becomes a prayer. And when a valid block does fail, treat it as information: the level the market should have defended, it did not. Lesson 8 shows how that failed block becomes a breaker.

COMMON MISTAKE

Marking blocks after the reaction. Scroll back through any chart and you will find a "perfect" block under every bounce — and you will not notice the forty that failed. Grade blocks before price returns, or do not count them.

Going deeper

Order block or gap — which is the entry? They usually sit next to each other, because the displacement candle that leaves the gap starts right at the block. The highest-quality entry zone in the framework is the overlap: a fresh A-grade block with a fresh gap directly above it (for longs). Entering at the gap gets more fills; entering at the block gets a better price and a tighter stop. As with gap conventions, choose one and test it.

The crowding problem, again. An A-grade block on a popular pair's H4 chart is drawn by a very large number of traders, with limit entries at its edge and stops just beyond it. By the framework's own logic, that is a liquidity pool. It is one reason textbook blocks sometimes fail by a few pips and then reverse — the same sweep mechanism, applied to the block's own followers. Your stop buffer exists for this.

Bodies or wicks? Wick-to-wick zones are wider and get touched more often; body-only zones are tighter and miss more. Neither is right. What is wrong is drawing wick-to-wick on one trade and body-only on the next because it "fits better".

Higher-timeframe blocks as context. A daily or H4 A-grade block is useful as a location — "this is an area where I will look for an M15 setup" — rather than as an entry in itself. That is the top-down process in Lesson 10.

What you are really testing. Blocks make claims you can count. Of fresh A-grade blocks on your pair and timeframe, how many produce a reaction of at least 1R before a close through? Does the sweep criterion matter? Does freshness? Fifty logged examples will tell you more than any amount of conviction.

THE RULES
  • Bullish OB: the last down-closing candle (or run) before displacement that leaves a fair value gap. Mirror for bearish.
  • Zone: block high to block low (or open to low — choose once). Invalid on a close beyond the far edge.
  • Grade before price returns: A = gap + sweep + structural break; B = gap + one; C = not marked.
  • Trade fresh A-grade blocks only, on the first touch.
  • Stop beyond the block's far edge plus about 10% of ATR; target the next untaken opposing pool; risk 0.5–1%.

Summary

  • An order block is the origin of a displaced move: a demand or supply zone with a sharper definition.
  • The gap above it is the evidence; without it there is no block.
  • Grade every candidate in advance on sweep, structure and gap. Trade A-grade, first touch only.
  • Refine large blocks with one fixed convention; never switch conventions to fit the trade.
  • Plan the failure before the touch: a close through the far edge ends the block and your stop is already there.

quiz.q: Which candle is the bullish order block?
options: The largest green candle in the rally
Any red candle in an uptrend
The last down-closing candle (or run) before a displaced move up that leaves a gap
The candle with the highest volume
quiz.why: The block is the origin of displacement. Without a displaced move and a gap, a red candle is just a red candle.

quiz.q: A candidate block has a fair value gap above it and the move broke structure, but nothing was swept. What grade is it?
quiz.why: Gap plus one of sweep or structure is B-grade under the course system.

quiz.q: When is a bullish order block invalid?
options: When a candle closes below the zone's low
quiz.why: A close beyond the far edge ends the block. Wicks into it are touches, not failures.

quiz.q: In the 'block that failed' example, which grading facts should have kept you out?
options: No sweep, no close above the prior high, and a downtrend context
The trade was taken in London
quiz.why: Without a sweep or structural break, inside a downtrend, it was not A-grade — and the strategy trades A-grade only.

quiz.q: Why does this course trade first touches only?
options: Each revisit uses up the zone and turns it into an obvious level that collects stops
Brokers widen spreads on second touches
quiz.why: On either story, interest is consumed on each visit, and the zone becomes a crowded pool itself.

quiz.q: What does 'the gap is the evidence, the order block is the inference' mean?
options: Gaps are more profitable than blocks
Blocks must always be inside gaps
The gap objectively shows displacement; the block is the zone we infer from it
quiz.why: The gap is mechanically defined proof of one-sided movement; the block is our inference about where that movement began.

lessons.title: Breaker Blocks — When a Failed Zone Flips
lessons.summary: Identify a breaker block with an objective five-step sequence, separate it from a weaker mitigation block, and trade the retest with a fixed stop and a pre-planned failure case.
lessons.html:
In Lesson 7 you planned for an order block to fail. This lesson is about what a failed block leaves behind.

When a well-defined zone breaks decisively, the traders who relied on it are now wrong, and the zone becomes a place they would like to get out at break-even. When price returns to that zone from the other side, it often reacts. Classical traders have called this "support becomes resistance" (and vice versa) for as long as there have been charts.
